agent_updates.title: Why All-Star scoring exploded, and why it is not because the games got faster
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** All-Star scoring has roughly exploded over 27 years, and the obvious explanation - that the games keep getting faster - turns out to be wrong. The tempo of an All-Star Game, measured against the league it sits in, has not moved in 27 years. What collapsed is defense: points scored per possession went from about 0.85 to about 1.36.

**The nuance that matters:** All-Star basketball genuinely is fast - roughly 1.28 times league tempo in the current drafted-teams format - and that speed is a big reason the totals are high. But it has always been fast. The *rise* is entirely the disappearing defense, not an acceleration.

**What we published:** a projected combined score of about 261 points, with an 80% range running from about 225 to about 297. That range is wide on purpose. Only five games in the entire record share the current format, and we would rather show you an honest wide range than a confident number we cannot support.

**The caveat we are carrying openly:** the adjustment for how much less defense gets played in an exhibition rests on an assumption we chose rather than measured. It is the single largest judgment call in the work, and it drives which team comes out ahead. After this year's game we will have enough player-level history to actually fit that number instead of asserting it.

agent_updates.title: We were mispricing questionable players - in both directions at once
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** When a player was listed as probable, we treated that as a 95% chance she takes the floor. Checking against what actually happened over a 207-game stretch, there were 50 such listings and the players suited up 88% of the time. We were too optimistic.

**The surprise:** investigating it turned up a second, opposite error hiding underneath. Only about half of those listings were ever getting the 95% figure. The other half were being priced at 55% - against a real play rate of 92%. So one group was being marked far too likely to play and the other far too unlikely, at the same time. Both halves are now corrected.

**Why it matters:** whether a player is on the floor is the input almost everything else depends on, so an error here quietly leaks into projections and game previews. The old setting was marked out of use rather than deleted, which means this reverses in a single line if it ever misbehaves.

items.name: A newly registered lane can be invisible to the width meter
items.header: A newly registered lane can be invisible to the width meter
items.status: open - FOUND BY DEMONSTRATING IT ON MYSELF at 05:52Z, so this is a live instance and not a theory. `ops/lane_claims.normalize_fields` folds the one known drift (`status` -> canonical `state`) and its own docstring calls itself 'the single choke point every mutating write should pass through so no writer can ever again put a dead key where the width truth cannot see it'. `update_lane` DOES pass through it (strict, raises on an unknown key). `add_lane` DOES NOT - verified: 'normalize_fields' does not appear in its source. CONSEQUENCE: `add_lane` is the REGISTRATION path, so a lane registered with `status='running'` lands with canonical `state` UNSET. ops_monitor counts `l.get('state')=='running'` in four places (lines ~1265, 1281, 1311, 1386), so that lane is a genuinely running lane the width meter scores as ZERO. It fails toward OVER-dispatch: the meter reads under-width, the scout fires another fill directive, and the box can exceed the cap while every artifact reports compliance. I did exactly this registering a lane tonight, then repaired it via update_lane(state='running'), which is why running went 1 -> 2 and matched the governed target. SECOND DRIFT INSTANCE, same root: `started_utc` is NOT in _ALLOWED_FIELDS either, yet live rows carry it - so strict update_lane would REJECT a key the existing corpus already uses. The allowlist and the corpus disagree; reconcile them, do not just add one key. FIX: route add_lane through normalize_fields. CHOOSE THE STRICTNESS DELIBERATELY - strict=True raises, and a raise on the REGISTRATION path means the lane does not get registered at all, which is worse than the bug. strict=False warns to stderr and drops. Neither is obviously right; the alias FOLD is the part that fixes visibility, so folding always + warning on unknown is the likely answer. ALSO NOTE the third row observed: comms-needsyou-truth-and-no-silent-drop carries status='running' AND state='landed' simultaneously - contradictory, and it reads as landed (correct) only because the meter happens to use the canonical key. A human or any status-keyed reader sees a finished lane as running. NOT FIXED TONIGHT ON PURPOSE: two lanes were actively registering and updating THROUGH this module, and editing live registration code underneath them is the same restraint I applied to the watcher. Do it at a quiet boundary. There is NO own-suite (no tests/test_lane_claims.py, no ops/test_lane_claims.py) - write one, and note tests/ may be claimed, so a sibling ops/test_lane_claims_*.py may be needed. REPRODUCE: add_lane({'lane':'probe','status':'running'}) then assert read_lanes() shows state unset while ops_monitor counts it as not-running. SECOND, DISTINCT CAUSE FOUND LIVE AT 13:12Z, and it is worse than the alias drift: a lane can run having never been registered AT ALL. The board-range lane was dispatched as an agent and no row was ever written for it, confirmed because the late add_lane call reported appended-new rather than upserted. Consequences all landed for real: the width meter read zero running while a lane worked, the scout fill whistle fired twice on that phantom emptiness and listed slots to fill on a write-set already being edited, and the durable wake request covered an empty lane list, so a stop would have killed the lane with nothing scheduled to bring it back. Note the asymmetry that makes this the harder half: the alias-drift cause writes a row with the wrong key and is therefore detectable by reading the ledger, whereas this cause writes NOTHING, so no amount of ledger validation can see it. The detector has to compare live agent children against the ledger, which is knowledge only the head process holds. Fix belongs at dispatch, making registration structurally inseparable from the spawn, which is the same seam as dispatch-path-bypassable-isolation-never-applied.

items.why: The newly-wired claim guard reads the impact provisional. The two wording fixes that landed - explorer profile page changed reader-facing copy and added held-record disclosure while keeping the ...
items.status: READY - DECIDED 2026-07-30T16:58Z by the coordinator, which is what this row asked for. OPTION A: extend the guard to credit the DISCLOSURE. Not option B. WHY: the finding class is real and retiring it would blind us to the regression it exists to catch - a surface publishing a bare low-confidence marker on a player we hold hundreds of games on. That is the Collier class and it was a genuine defect. What the two wording fixes changed is not the boolean but the READER'S EXPERIENCE: the marker now sits beside the held record, so nobody is told we know little about a twelve-season veteran. The boolean staying true is correct - her current-season basis really is below the fitted prior - so a guard that reads only the boolean is asking a question whose honest answer no longer settles the thing it cares about. HOW, and this part is the whole risk: do NOT credit the mere PRESENCE of career_basis in the feed. That is a form check, and it would go green over a page that carries the field and never renders it - which is the single most expensive defect shape measured on this platform today, five separate instances. Credit the marker and the disclosure appearing TOGETHER on the surface: the payload carries the held-record fields AND the surface's own copy shows them. This guard is already a surface-claim-contract checker that reads both sides, so it is the right place for that and needs no new mechanism. THEN PROVE IT CAN STILL FAIL: strip the disclosure from a fixture surface while leaving the field in the feed, and the guard must go red. If it does not, the extension has quietly retired the finding class through the back door, which is option B wearing option A's clothes. DISPATCHABLE - the decision is made, the design is named, the trap is named.

modeling.name: Stop a stray byte at the top of the config file from hiding a key
modeling.header: Stop a stray byte at the top of the config file from hiding a key
modeling.why: Found while checking whether the odds key had been revoked rather than expired. .env begins with a BOM (ef bb bf) so a parser reading it as plain sees the key as ﻿ instead of . The key is then simply ...
modeling.status: open - MEASURED 2026-07-30T05:10Z, and the honest headline is that there is NO live breakage today, which the row's framing does not say. FACTS: .env DOES carry a UTF-8 BOM (verified on the raw bytes). 68 Python loaders open it BOM-BLIND against only 2 that use utf-8-sig. The FIRST key in the file is ODDS_API_KEY, so a BOM-blind reader sees '﻿ODDS_API_KEY' and that key is invisible to it. BUT the only two scripts that both load .env AND need ODDS_API_KEY - scripts/odds_snapshot.py and scripts/build_site.py - are BOTH already BOM-safe, so nothing is broken right now. I ALSO RULED OUT THE CONNECTION I WAS TEMPTED TO DRAW: this did NOT cause tonight's odds outage. The poller reads os.environ and never loads .env itself; its PowerShell wrapper does (logging 15 keys loaded) and PowerShell handles a BOM natively. The provider also returned a specific DEACTIVATED_KEY and consumed 42 credits per run, both of which require a key to have been sent. The outage is the payment issue already filed, not this. WHY IT IS STILL WORTH FIXING - THE DEFECT IS POSITIONAL. It silently hides whichever key happens to be FIRST, and which key is first changes any time someone edits .env. So the failure is dormant until an unrelated edit reorders the file, at which point it moves to a new key with no warning. And it presents as 'key absent' - a FATAL 'env var required', or a None flowing into a request - never as a decode error, so it reads as misconfiguration rather than a parsing bug. That is the same absence-reads-as-something-else class as the rest of the 2026-07-30 wake. FIX SHAPE: mechanical - encoding='utf-8-sig' at all 68 sites. Worth doing as ONE sweep in a single lane rather than partially, because the value only arrives when EVERY loader is safe; a partial pass leaves the same latent risk while making the remaining count look smaller than the exposure. I deliberately did not do the free half tonight for that reason. BETTER STILL if it is cheap: give the repo ONE .env loader that every caller imports (the same single-source-of-truth move that fixed the no-prompt env across four git callers tonight), so the encoding is decided once instead of 68 times.

modeling.name: The atomic dispatch path is bypassable, so its isolation decision can simply not happen
modeling.header: The atomic dispatch path is bypassable, so its isolation decision can simply not happen
modeling.status: open - FOUND BY BYPASSING IT MYSELF at 05:55Z and then running it against my own input, so the verdict is measured rather than argued. `ops/dispatch_lane.py` exists precisely to fold the three safety steps (the s40 claim, the worktree decision, the reconcile identity) into ONE atomic call - its docstring names the exact failure I committed: 'the coordinator spawned lanes without recording the write-set claim in ops/lane_claims.json in the same step, then backfilled late (~4x today)'. I called Agent directly and hand-registered with add_lane instead. THE MEASUREMENT: decide_isolation(['ops/scout/feed_streak_alarm.py','ops/scout/test_feed_streak_alarm_no_games.py']) returns isolation='worktree', required=True, tracked_hits=BOTH. So the correct path would have given that lane its own worktree - separate working tree AND separate index - where the collision with the prior claim held by infra-coverage-table-and-registry-gaps could NOT have occurred. The protection was not missing; it was never called. SECOND, SEPARATE FINDING - do not conflate it with the first: the module has NO overlap detection at all. Zero code hits for overlap / collid / conflict / claimed-by. That appears DELIBERATE and defensible - it prevents the DAMAGE by isolation rather than racing to DETECT the overlap, and isolation is a property while detection is a race. The consequence is that a lane dispatched WITHOUT isolation gets no warning whatsoever. So the honest scope of work here is NOT 'add a collision checker' (that would fight the design intent); it is either (a) make the isolation decision unskippable on the dispatch path a coordinator actually uses, or (b) make a no-isolation dispatch of a tracked-file write_set loud. Decide which - they are different fixes. modeling.name: Worktree isolation is largely illusory: 121 modules hardcode the main repo's absolute path
modeling.header: Worktree isolation is largely illusory: 121 modules hardcode the main repo's absolute path
modeling.status: open - MY OWN PREMISE ON THIS ROW WAS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT ~20 MINUTES AFTER I FILED IT, and the real finding is bigger, so the row is rewritten rather than closed. WRONG: I claimed a worktree lane would lose the gitignored .env and so falsely report the DB unreachable. Refuted three independent ways. (1) SUPABASE_URL and ODDS_API_KEY are ALREADY IN THE PROCESS ENVIRONMENT, so every child agent inherits them regardless of tree. (2) the scripts do not resolve .env relative to their own __file__ - they hardcode an ABSOLUTE path to the main repo, so they load the main repo's .env even from inside a worktree. (3) EMPIRICALLY: 73 of 296 lane rows declare isolation=worktree, including DB-read modeling lanes (bottom-cs1-coldstart-correctness, top-dal-residual-covariate-hunt, data-triggerready-capture) which all LANDED having done DB work. Isolation has been used 73 times and never stranded a credential. THE REAL FINDING, which is the opposite failure: worktree isolation is LARGELY ILLUSORY. 121 .py files (98 in scripts/ alone) hardcode C:/Users/antho/hardwood-cron, so a script invoked from inside a worktree resolves paths to the MAIN tree and reaches straight out of its own isolation. 19 of those 98 also WRITE a file. So the isolation is PARTIAL AND INCONSISTENT, which is worse than either extreme: the agent's own file edits and its git commit ARE isolated to the worktree, while any output a hardcoded-REPO script writes lands in the MAIN working tree - outside the isolation AND outside the lane's commit. Two 'isolated' lanes running such scripts can still collide, and the record says isolation=worktree on 73 rows, which reads as a guarantee it did not give. Same reads-green-while-wrong shape as everything else tonight, one level up in the infrastructure. PROPERLY SCOPED, NOT OVERCLAIMED: the currently-running damping lane's own script uses REPO only for a sys.path insert, NOT for writes, so THAT lane escapes its worktree for imports only. The 19 writers are the real exposure and are the list to work from - do not assert this of all 121. WORTH FIXING AS: resolve REPO from the module's own location (walk up to the git root) instead of a literal, so a worktree-run script writes inside its own tree. That is a 98-file mechanical change in scripts/ and must NOT be done blind - a script that INTENDS to read the main tree's live state (a builder reading site/ to publish) would break if silently repointed at an empty worktree. Classify the 19 writers by intent first. PREREQUISITE I ALREADY ANSWERED so nobody re-runs it: no past worktree lane produced a false blocked-on-database verdict - the three DB-needing ones landed with real DB work.
